Testimony In Support of

LD 1574 An Act to Amend the Credit for Educational Opportunity and Student Loan
Repayment Tax Credit
Good Afternoon Senator Grohoski, Rep. Cloutier and Members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Taxation. I am State Representative Caldwell Jackson of District 80 representing the towns of
Oxford, Otisfield, Buckfield and Hebron. I am here to present LD 1574 An Act to Amend the
Credit for Educational Opportunity and Student Loan Repayment Tax Credit.
This bill allows qualified student borrowers to make early payments on eligible student loans for taxable years begimiing on or after January l, 2026, so that a qualified individual with unused carryover credits may carry over and apply to the credit amount allowed, the portion, as reduced
from year to year, of any unused credits until the tax credit is entirely depleted.
This basically amends the existing educational opportunity and student loan repayment tax credit to make it a little easier for students to repay their loans.
I hope you can support this amendment.

190400:
Thank you for your support of LD 1574 An Act to Amend the Credit for Educational
Opportunity and Student Loan Repayment Tax Credit.
My wife and I were inspired to suggest this amendment to Representative Jackson after learning about the student loan repayment tax credit. My wife and l worked hard and made sacrifices in order to save enough money to pay off her student loans as quickly as possible. Just before reaching our lump sum savings goal we discovered the student
loan tax credit. We were excited that we would be able to keep some of our hard earned
money to help purchase our first home (especially considering the market conditions)
and then start a family.
However, we soon discovered that in order to redeem the full value of the student loan tax credit we would need to space our payments out over the course of 10 years despite the fact that we could pay them off in their entirety now. This meant we would need to
maintain those student loans and incur the interest costs. In addition it meant that our
debt to income ratio would be impacted and that financing a home (or car, etc.) would
be significantly limited. By allowing individuals to pay off their student loans early and redeem an annual state income tax credit up to $2500 for 10 years, hardworking individuals in Maine will be incentivized to pay off their loans ahead of time and rewarded with lower total interest paid and an increased ability to finance homes,
vehicles, etc.
With this amendment the income tax credit will be more effective in its goal to attract college graduates to join the workforce in Maine, buy homes in Maine, and make investments in Maine. lt will also incentivize them to stay in Maine if they make early payments in order to obtain their annual tax credit. lt can also help individuals overcome a barrier to home ownership in an already challenging market or make investments in
small business ventures that support our economy.
Thank you for your thoughtful consideration of this testimony, we are looking forward to
making our final student loan payment soon!

TESTIMONY OF MICHAEL J. ALLEN, ASSOCIATE COMMISSIONER FOR TAX POLICY
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Taxation Hearing Date: April 16, 2025
LD 1574 - "An Act to Amend the Credit for Educational Opportunity and Student Loan Repayment Tax Credit"
Senator Grohoski, Representative Cloutier, and members of the Taxation Committee - good afternoon, my name is Michael Allen, Associate Commissioner for Tax Policy in the Department of Administrative and Financial Services. I am testifying at the request of the Administration Against LD 1574, "An Act to Amend the Credit for Educational Opportunity and Student Loan Repayment Tax Credit."
This bill would eliminate the carry forward of unused educational opportunity tax credit (EOTC) from the calculation of the student loan repayment tax credit (SLRTC) amount allowed for tax years beginning after 2025 (currently allowed to be carried forward through tax year 2026). For tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, the bill also proposes to allow qualified individuals with unused carryover credits to carry over and apply the portion of unused credits to the SLRTC.
The bill summary indicates that the intent of the bill is to allow early payments of eligible student loans that may be applied to the maximum SLRTC and to carry the relevant credit forward each year until entirely depleted. However, the bill language does not clearly implement this intent.
For tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2022, the EOTC was replaced by the SLRTC. Currently, the refundable SLRTC is equal to the amount of
1

education loan payments made by the individual directly to the lender during the tax year plus, for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2022, and before January 1, 2027, any amount of unused EOTC carried forward from prior tax years that does not exceed the 10-year carry forward limit. The credit is limited to $2,500 annually, up to $25,000 lifetime, per taxpayer.
The EOTC program was replaced by the SLRTC program to eliminate ambiguity associated with the program for taxpayers, including allowing consistent refundability for all qualified individuals and eliminating carry forward of unused credits, as well as to ease the compliance and administrative difficulties relative to preparing and processing credit claims. The SLRTC is much less complicated than the EOTC and this simplicity has made the program more accessible to taxpayers and easier to administer, in short it has been working well since it became effective in 2022.
The SLTRTC is a unique and generous credit and changes to the credit should be carefully considered.
The Administration also notes the following technical concerns:
 Section 1 of the bill is unnecessary and should be removed. 36 MRSA � 5217-D(2)(B) applies only to tax years beginning before January 1, 2022.
 Section 2 of the bill is unclear, and does not accomplish the changes described in the bill summary.
The full fiscal impact estimate is not available at this time, but according to preliminary estimates the bill would cost approximately $3-$4 million dollars even if borrowers do not change their repayment behavior in response to the bill. Notably, this assessment is based on one interpretation of the purpose of the bill.
2

The preliminary estimated administrative costs are under review. However, computer programming costs will be required to accommodate the carry forward of unused credits.
The Administration looks forward to working with the Committee on the bill; representatives from MRS will be here for the Work Session to provide additional information and respond in detail to the Committee's questions.
